Duke Ellington was one of the most important musicians, composers, and bandleaders in all jazz history. And this recording of this song is where his unique voice was born. He had recorded a few times in the years prior to this, but this is the first piece that sounds like Ellington and could not have been written by anyone else.

Some of the features that make it distinctively his include the apparently loose, wandering way the instruments seem to be playing, as well as the way the melody at first seems to be different episodes, yet tells one coherent story.

And story telling was important to Ellington. While his claim that he always started with a story and developed the music from that was demonstrably false, his pieces do come together and when he supplies the story --- "East St. Louis Toodle-Oo", in his telling, is about a man walking home at the end of a hard day of work, looking forward to the hot meal he knows his wife has waiting for him --- it pretty much always enhances the music.

Not long after this recording, Ellington and his band landed the gig that made them nation-wide stars. They became the house band at The Cotton Club, an exclusive club in the heart of Harlem that catered to exclusively white clientele, offering them an "authentic Harlem" experience. The floor shows continue to be famous today, and the music from them was broadcast live over radio, first to New York, and soon across the nation. Unfortunately, given the technology of the time, these broadcasts were not recorded, and could not have been, at least in their entirety.

When Ellington and his band ended their contract to tour the country instead, Cab Calloway was the next bandleader at The Cotton Club.
